blurb: From Turing's big question through two "AI winters" to deep learning and the chatbot era.

steps.p: In 1950 Alan Turing proposed a test: if a judge chatting by text can't tell a machine from a person, call it intelligent.
steps.analogy: A blind interview — judge only by the conversation.

steps.p: In 1956 John McCarthy coined "artificial intelligence" for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College, hoping for big progress in two months.
Programs proved maths theorems, played checkers and solved puzzles. Researchers predicted human-level AI within a generation.
In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA imitated a therapist by turning your words back into questions: "I feel sad" → "Why do you feel sad?"
People felt understood by ELIZA despite it understanding nothing — the first sign of how easily we read minds into machines.

cards.why: John McCarthy, in the 1955 proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop. He later created the programming language Lisp.

cards.statement: The Dartmouth proposal suggested big progress could be made in a single summer.
cards.why: True. It hoped "a significant advance" could be made by a small group in two months. It took decades.

options: A judge, chatting by text, can tell a machine from a person
A machine can copy a painting
A robot can walk like a person
cards.why: Can you tell? Turing swapped the vague question "can machines think?" for a test you could actually run.

cards.title: ELIZA's creator was disturbed when his secretary asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it privately.
cards.detail: Joseph Weizenbaum's simple program only reflected users' words back. People's emotional attachment to it made him a lifelong critic of over-trusting computers.

cards.statement: ELIZA understood the meaning of what users typed.
cards.why: False. It matched keywords and filled templates. The understanding was all in the user's head — the "ELIZA effect".

steps.p: Early AI worked on toy problems but collapsed on messy real ones. Computers were also far too weak.
In 1973 a UK report by James Lighthill judged AI a failure, and funding was cut in Britain and America. Research went cold for years.
In the 1980s companies built expert systems: thousands of if-then rules written down from human experts — "if the part is X and the order is Y, then add Z".
Rules couldn't cover every case, were costly to update and broke on anything unexpected. A second winter followed in the late 1980s.
steps.analogy: Like trying to teach someone to cook by writing a rule for every possible kitchen situation.

steps.p: Meanwhile a few researchers kept working on neural networks, even when it was unfashionable. Their persistence paid off decades later.

cards.q: The 1973 Lighthill Report in the UK led to…
options: Deep cuts to AI research funding
cards.why: Funding cuts. It concluded AI hadn't delivered on its promises, helping trigger the first "AI winter".

options: Applying large sets of hand-written if-then rules from human experts
cards.why: Hand-written rules. Knowledge had to be typed in by people — the opposite of today's learn-from-data approach.

cards.title: DEC's XCON expert system configured computer orders and was reported to save the company around $25 million a year.
cards.detail: It checked that each VAX computer order had compatible parts. Its success fuelled the 1980s boom — but it needed constant maintenance as products changed.

cards.statement: IBM's Deep Blue, which beat Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, was a neural network.
cards.why: False. It used specialised chips to search about 200 million positions a second, with hand-tuned evaluation rules. Brute force, not learning.

cards.statement: Neural network research continued through the AI winters, even when unfashionable.
cards.why: True. Researchers like Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio kept going — and later won the Turing Award for it.

steps.p: Neural networks and backpropagation existed since the 1980s. What was missing was fuel.
The internet produced huge labelled datasets like ImageNet — 14 million photos — led by Fei-Fei Li.
GPUs, built for video games, turned out to be perfect for the maths of neural networks.
Tricks like ReLU and dropout made deep networks — many layers — train reliably.
In 2012 AlexNet crushed an image-recognition contest. Within a few years deep learning took over vision, speech and translation.
steps.analogy: A car design that had sat in a garage for decades — until someone finally supplied fuel and a road.

cards.q: The 2018 Turing Award, computing's top honour, went to which three deep-learning pioneers?
cards.why: Hinton, LeCun and Bengio — the trio who kept faith in neural networks through the winters.

cards.statement: Yann LeCun's convolutional networks were reading handwritten cheques commercially in the 1990s.
cards.why: True. Systems from AT&T Bell Labs processed a significant share of US cheques — deep learning working quietly, decades early.

cards.q: Who led the creation of the ImageNet dataset?
cards.why: Fei-Fei Li. Many doubted a giant dataset was worth the effort; it became the proving ground for deep learning.

cards.title: Geoffrey Hinton and John Hopfield won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational work on neural networks.
cards.detail: The prize recognised Hopfield networks and Hinton's Boltzmann machines, which drew on ideas from physics.

cards.q: The "deep" in deep learning refers to…
cards.why: Many layers. Each layer builds on the last, from edges to shapes to objects.

steps.p: In 2017 Google researchers published "Attention Is All You Need", introducing the transformer — the design behind every modern chatbot.
Models like BERT (2018) and GPT showed you could pretrain on huge amounts of text, then adapt to many tasks.
GPT-1 (2018) had 117 million parameters; GPT-3 (2020) had 175 billion — about 1,500 times more in two years.
In November 2022 ChatGPT put a post-trained model in a simple chat box, and AI went mainstream almost overnight.
Since then: models that see and hear, reasoning models that think first (2024), and agents that act.

cards.why: 2018 → 2020 → 2022 → 2024. Pretraining, then scale, then chat, then reasoning.

cards.statement: In 2019, OpenAI initially held back the full GPT-2 model over concerns about misuse.
cards.why: True. It released smaller versions first, worried about fake news. The full model came out nine months later.

cards.title: GPT-3 had about 1,500 times more parameters than GPT-1, just two years earlier.
cards.detail: GPT-1 (2018) had 117 million; GPT-3 (2020) had 175 billion. That pace of scaling was unprecedented in computing.

cards.q: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for…
cards.why: AlphaFold. It predicts a protein's 3D shape from its building-block sequence — a 50-year-old problem in biology.

cards.title: Read the paper that started it
cards.body: "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) is short, and its introduction is readable even without maths.
cards.challenge: Search for the paper and read just its abstract and first page. Spot one idea you learned in this course.
